newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: After trade talks, Japan seeks to step from shadows.
newsitem.headline: After trade talks, Japan seeks to step from shadows.

text.p: Tokyo hardly hogged the limelight at this week's gathering of a pivotal world trade organisation, but some Japanese officials think the time has come to step out of the shadows.

Ministers from World Trade Organisation (WTO) on Friday sealed a sweeping pact to free commerce in information technology, help the poor and set the agenda of world trade talks for the rest of the century.
The accord followed a week of intense and often acrimonious negotiations among the 128-member world trade watchdog, an organisation whose praises Tokyo has sung loudly.

"Some people might say that Japan may be situated in a peculiar position to be a bridge and mediate differences between nations," Hiroshi Hosokawa, Vice Trade Minister for International Affairs told Reuters after the meeting ended on Friday.
"My view is somewhat different -- Japan itself must have its national interests, and those ought to be expressed more explicitly," Hosokawa said.
Japan's aspirations to play a high-profile role at the WTO's first ministerial conference here this week suffered when its trade minister was trapped at home by a scandal at his ministry.
Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, originally set for a one-day appearance, extended his visit in an apparent effort to allay concerns Japan was giving free trade short shrift.
Hosokawa said, however, that no delegates had questioned Tokyo's commitment to the WTO.
Trade minister Shinji Sato's no-show "was an unfortunate incident," Hosokawa said. "But they all know why he had to be kept at home."

Despite Japan's low profile at the conference, where Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky and European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan often stole the show by trading public barbs, Tokyo achieved most of its main objectives.
"It wasn't 100 percent, but it was a good outcome," one senior trade official said.
High on Japan's list was a ground-breaking Information Technology Agreement (ITA) to scrap tariffs in the fast growing $600 billion world market for computer-related goods.
Washington led the push to clinch the infotech deal, with strong backing from Tokyo.
"We certainly share the view that the ITA is one of the major achievements," Hosokawa said.

Hosokawa said the ITA deal, so far joined by 28 countries accounting for over 80 percent of world trade in the sector, would benefit both exporters and Asian countries whose markets for such goods are the world's fastest growing.

"People tend to look only at the impact on exporting opportunities...but I don't take that sort of view," Hosokawa said. "Countries that eliminate the tariffs would also benefit because the countries and consumers can have easier access to foreign-made information technologies."

Hosokawa said Japan was also pleased with a WTO decision to expand its agenda by creating two new groups to study the issues of treatment of foreign investment and competition -- although a dispute over what the latter entailed already appeared to be brewing.

Tokyo had argued that talks on competition policy should include anti-dumping measures and special tariffs, while Washington and Brussels -- the main practitioners of anti-dumping steps -- were against linking the two.
"The anti-dumping laws are not on the table," Barshefsky told a news conference after the release of the WTO's ministerial declaration on Friday.
Japanese officials begged to differ.
"What she (Barshefsky) said is not correct," Nobutoshi Akao, Japan's ambassador to international organisations in Geneva told a separate news conference.
